subject: best practice for estimating missing data

messages.author: 2430f2828c808219
messages.subject: best practice for estimating missing data
parts:
Hi all

I am frequently faced with missing data.  Often, I need to use these data as predictors, so I need to find ways to estimate them.  Ideally, the estimation of missing values occurs in a way that does not feedback into the underlying probability model for which these data are being used.  In other words, the missing data are treated as an "observable function" or a type of "observed data".  I know how to do this in BUGS, and to a lesser extent in JAGS (see discussion here http://jackman.stanford.edu/blog/?p=1199), but the approach in STAN is still unclear to me.

I have tried to derive an example to demonstrate an application for this problem.  Attached is a R script that generates a dataset with missing values.  I've then followed a rather simplistic approach, where I fit a model to predict the observed data, use this model to estimate the missing values, and then patch together the missing and observed values into one vector to use as a predictor in another subsequent model.  What ends up happening is that I'm generating biased estimates, whereby I over-estimate the residual variance of my missing data (sigmaChb in the attached) and underestimate the effect of the predictor for the observed values (= lambda[1]).  I  guess that this is to be expected given the way I've written my model?...  

My question is how would I write my model in STAN to get closer to the original "known" values that I used to create the original dataset?  Presumably, I would have to remove "chaob_miss_err" from the model block in the attached file, but sampling can't be done elsewhere.  Simply removing the residual error (chaob_miss_err) and dropping the missing values on the "mean" relationship doesn't address this problem either...

Again, thank you for your time, and particularly your patience with my questions.  I am an ecologist and have no formal training in statistics or computer science, so think of me as someone trying to speak a foreign language they learned by watching many re-runs of "Friends" on late-night TV.  I can communicate fairly well at this stage, but sometimes, things still get lost in translation.

Andrew

In other words, it would draw from the joint posterior distribution of the missing data and the unknown parameters. However, the handling of missing values in the current version of Stan is not ideal, to be honest with you.

My question is how would I write my model in STAN to get closer to the original "known" values that I used to create the original dataset?  Presumably, I would have to remove "chaob_miss_err" from the model block in the attached file, but sampling can't be done elsewhere.  Simply removing the residual error (chaob_miss_err) and dropping the missing values on the "mean" relationship doesn't address this problem either...

There is a chapter on missing data in the Stan reference manual (currently chapter 7) that has a Gaussian example where the likelihood is split into two blocks, one for the observed values and one for the missing values. Can you recast your example (and maybe make it simpler) so that it is similar to the example in the reference manual? And then if there is still a problem, we can go from there.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: best practice for estimating missing data
parts: On Saturday, October 6, 2012 5:02:21 PM UTC-4, atzap wrote:

This statement seems odd to me in that I think one virtue of (a future release of) Stan is that it would estimate the distribution of missing values in a way that is consistent with the probability model for which the data are being used. In other words, it would draw from the joint posterior distribution of the missing data and the unknown parameters. Otherwise, the estimates of the parameters would be biased, except under very restrictive assumptions about the missingness mechanism. However, the handling of missing values in the current version of Stan is not ideal, to be honest with you.

But this isn't what is happening now though eh?...  Ultimately, I think I might be phrasing my question poorly.  Given the current handling of missing values, what is the best approach for recovering the original parameter estimates used to derive the data in my example?  My current attempts to model this in STAN lead to rather biased inference.

Stan is capable of doing what I would consider to be the right approach, but it is not particularly convenient to deal with missing data. In a real dataset, there is likely to be missingness scattered throughout several variables, so it is hard to just split the data up into observed blocks and missing blocks.

In your case, I believe that your .stan code is correct, but there was a bug in the R code that generated the data. In this line

bdat$y <- rbinom(bdat$N, bdat$n, plogis(-3 + .4 * bdat$chaob))

bdat$chaob is of length 20, while bdat$N is 120 and bdat$n is of length 120. What happens in these situations is that R "recycles" plogis(-3 + .4 * bdat$chaob) five times in order to provide 120 probabilities. In other words, the probabilities for the 20 observed data points are also being used for the 100 missing data points, which is inconsistent with the intended model.

If you change it to

bdat$y <- rbinom(bdat$N, bdat$n, plogis(-3 + .4 * chaob_act))

then, Stan seems to yield reasonable estimates. You can verify that the MLEs are close to what you intended with

mle <- glm(cbind(bdat$y, bdat$n - bdat$y) ~ chaob_act, family = binomial())
summary(mle)

These sorts of subtle bugs can be reduced by using odd numbers for sample sizes because recycling will trigger a warning.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: best practice for estimating missing data
parts:
On 10/7/12 3:28 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Stan is capable of doing what I would consider to be the right approach,

Basically the same thing as BUGS does -- use the joint
posterior with the missing data as "parameters". You
need to model the missigness yourself, though, with data
missing completely at random being the baseline.

> but it is not particularly convenient to deal
> with missing data. In a real dataset, there is likely to be missingness scattered throughout several variables, so it is
> hard to just split the data up into observed blocks and missing blocks.

You can split each variable into observed and missing
components, put everything back together in a transformed
param, and you're good to go (though it's not the most
efficient approach imaginable). You can do this variable
by variables, so rather than potentially 2^N missigness patterns
for N predictors, you only have to deal with N parameters.

Unfortunately, that's still N ugly index fiddles, which
wouldn't be that bad if they weren't so error-prone to
write and difficult to debug.

- Bob

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: best practice for estimating missing data
parts:
On Monday, October 8, 2012 11:51:14 AM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
You can split each variable into observed and missing
components, put everything back together in a transformed
param, and you're good to go (though it's not the most
efficient approach imaginable).

I was playing with this approach over the weekend, benchmarking against the data splitting approach shown in the manual. Merging the imputed values into the right places in the mixed vector presents some obstacles. I found a quick solution, but I'm hoping there's a better algorithm in the transformed parameters that Bob and the other real programmers might suggest.

First, here are my parameters and transformed parameters blocks:
    parameters {
        real<lower=0> sigma;
        real alpha;
        real beta;
        real x_miss[N_miss];        // imputed x values
        real x_mu;                  // mean of dist of x values
        real<lower=0> x_sigma;      // sd of dist of x values
    }
    transformed parameters {
        real x_impute[N];
        for ( i in 1:N ) {
            x_impute[i] <- x[i];
            for ( g in 1:(x_is_miss[i]) ) {
                x_impute[i] <- x_miss[ x_missidx[i] ];
            }
        }
    }

So x_impute will hold a mix of observed values and imputed values. x_is_miss is 0/1 indicator of missing x. The trick for me was getting the parameters inserted into the right spots, so I ended up using x_missidx (passed as data, length N_miss) to hold the proper indices. Feels like a hack, but it works. I also had to use that for() trick to simulate if().

The above approach works, producing the same inferences as the data splitting approach, but does run a bit slower. I used simulated data of 1000 observed y's and 800 observed x's in a simple linear regression (so imputed 200 values). Call the approach above the "vector merging" approach. 10k samples (1k warmup) took:

   user  system elapsed 
 61.975   1.107  62.967 

The data splitting approach took instead:

   user  system elapsed 
 57.367   1.091  58.140 

I'll attach the entire script that defines both versions of the model, in case it's helpful to others.

I understand the necessity to use increment_log_prob() instead of the sampling operator "~" when we define a sampling distribution for a transformed parameter (or unknown in general, like missing data), so I have no complaint about the appearance of the warning message.  But the "transformed" data here is simply a merged matrix of observed data (x) and unknowns from the parameters block (x_miss), neither of which are actually transformed from their observed or unknown/sampled values.  So in this instance, can I simply ignore the warning?  That is, I assume there is no actual need for increment_log_prob() since I can think of no adjustment required for the Jacobian.  Is that correct?

The parser can't really tell the difference between a non-linear transformation and a linear transformation, much less an identity "transformation". So, just ignore the warning when you are sure there is no transforming going on. Or consider a linear transformation to be a special case of a non-linear transformation, in which case you "need" to increment_log_prob() by a constant (log(1) in your case) that has no effect on the MCMC and can be ignored like every other constant that Stan ignores.

Ben

indexing of parameters and some known linear functions applied

execution to see what transform's done.
